title: VPNs & Secure Remote Access
summary: How traditional VPNs grant network-level trust through an encrypted tunnel, and why that all-or-nothing model is being displaced by zero trust.

slides.markdown:
A **VPN (virtual private network)** does two things at once: it encrypts your traffic in transit, and it makes your device look like it's *inside* a private network it isn't physically connected to. Those are separable ideas, but classic VPNs bundle them.

For decades this was how remote workers reached internal systems, and how offices connected to each other over the public internet. It still is, widely.

The catch is the second half of that bundle: "looks like it's inside the network" usually means **broad network-level trust**, not access to one specific app. That single design choice is why VPNs are increasingly viewed as a legacy pattern — and why understanding exactly what they grant is the real interview substance here, more than the encryption.

slides.subTitle: An encrypted tunnel plus network membership
slides.markdown:
Strip away the marketing and a VPN is two mechanisms stacked together:

- **An encrypted tunnel.** Your traffic is wrapped so anyone observing the wire between you and the VPN gateway sees ciphertext, not your requests.
- **Network membership.** Once the tunnel is up, your device is assigned an IP on the private network (or is treated as if it were), so it can reach internal hosts the same way a machine physically plugged into the office network could.

The encryption is the part most people focus on, but the membership is the part with the bigger security consequence: it's a coarse, all-or-nothing grant. Once connected, you're generally not re-checked per request — you're just "on the network" the way anyone plugged into an office ethernet port would be.

| | Site-to-site VPN | Remote-access VPN |
|---|---|---|
| Connects | Two networks (e.g. office to data center, or office to cloud VPC) | One device to a network |
| Endpoints | Gateway devices/routers on each end | A client app on a laptop/phone plus a gateway |
| Typical use | Branch office reaching HQ or a cloud region, always-on | An employee working from home or travel, on demand |
| Traffic pattern | Steady, bidirectional, many users behind each end | One user's traffic, on and off through the day |

Both rely on the same underlying tunneling and encryption, the difference is *who* is on each end. A site-to-site VPN is effectively permanent network glue between two locations; a remote-access VPN is a single device dialing in, which is the pattern most relevant to "how does an employee reach internal tools from home."

| | IPSec VPN | SSL/TLS VPN |
|---|---|---|
| Layer | Network layer (wraps IP packets) | Transport/application layer, over TLS |
| Client | Usually needs dedicated client software | Often just a browser, or a lightweight client |
| What it exposes | Whole-network access once connected | Can be scoped to specific apps (a portal listing allowed internal services) more naturally |
| Common use | Site-to-site, always-on tunnels | Remote-access for individual users, easier to deploy widely |

IPSec operates low enough in the stack that it tunnels arbitrary IP traffic — great for connecting whole networks, but that also means it defaults to giving broad reachability once connected. SSL/TLS VPNs (and their descendants like clientless web portals) sit higher up, which makes it more natural to scope access to a specific set of applications rather than the whole subnet — a step in the direction zero trust takes further.

slides.subTitle: Once connected, broad network access
slides.markdown:
Here's the core design flaw interviewers want you to name: a VPN authenticates you **once, at connection time**, and then treats your traffic as trusted network traffic for the rest of the session. It typically doesn't re-verify who you are, what device you're on, or whether that device's posture (patched, not infected, disk encrypted) is still acceptable five minutes into the session.

And the grant itself is usually broad — "on the corporate VPN" often means reachability to a wide swath of internal IP space, not just the two apps you actually need for your job. This is a case of the network substituting for identity: proving you can reach the tunnel is treated as proof you should be trusted, which is a much weaker claim than it sounds.

This is exactly the gap that made VPN credentials such a common target: steal one set of VPN credentials (phishing, credential stuffing, an unpatched VPN appliance) and you inherit that same broad, un-re-checked network access.

slides.sectionTitle: A remote-access tunnel into the office
slides.markdown:
![A laptop connects through an encrypted tunnel to a VPN gateway, which fans out to file server, wiki, and database with no further check at the gateway](assets/vpn-flat-network.svg)

The diagram is the whole argument in one picture: encryption protects the pipe, but everything downstream of the gateway is reachable the moment the tunnel is up, with no additional identity or device check baked into that reachability. Whatever the gateway's ACLs allow, the connected device gets — for the whole session.

slides.sectionTitle: Split tunneling and the shared-blast-radius problem
slides.markdown:
**Split tunneling** lets some of a device's traffic go through the VPN (to reach internal resources) while the rest goes directly to the internet (to save bandwidth and avoid routing, say, video calls through a corporate gateway). It's a real performance and cost trade-off, but it also means the device is simultaneously exposed to the open internet *and* holds a live, trusted tunnel into the internal network.

A device compromised through its direct internet traffic — a malicious download, a drive-by exploit — now sits on the same laptop as the trusted VPN session, and can potentially ride that session inward. Full tunneling (routing everything through the VPN) avoids this at the cost of bandwidth and centralized egress monitoring load.

This is the same underlying issue as the VPN trust problem, one layer down: the tunnel doesn't know or care what else the device is doing at the same time.

slides.sectionTitle: VPN concentrators as a single point of compromise
slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
VPN gateways (concentrators) are internet-facing, run complex parsing code, and hold the keys to internal network access — which makes them one of the highest-value single targets in a network. Several major real-world intrusions in the last decade started with an unpatched or misconfigured VPN appliance, not a phished end user at all.

That concentrates risk in an unusual way: a vulnerability in one appliance can be worth more to an attacker than any individual credential, because compromising the gateway itself can grant a path around authentication entirely, or expose every session's traffic. This is a large part of the modern argument for zero trust: instead of one perimeter device that, if broken, opens the whole network, distribute trust decisions to a policy engine that checks identity and posture on every request, so no single box is that valuable a target.

Operationally, this also means VPN appliance patching should be treated with the urgency of a public-facing server, not routine IT maintenance — it usually gets far less scrutiny than that risk deserves.

The pitfall to name directly: assuming that because traffic arrived over the VPN, it's safe to trust more than traffic arriving any other way. "On the VPN" tells you the tunnel was authenticated at connection time — it tells you nothing about whether the device is currently compromised, whether the same employee is still the one typing, or whether that employee's laptop just picked up malware from a phishing link five minutes ago over a split-tunneled connection.

Teams that build internal services with looser authentication "because it's only reachable from the VPN" are making exactly this mistake — they've quietly made the VPN gateway's one-time check the *only* check standing between the internet and that service, once a session or credential is stolen.

The fix — covered later in this group under zero trust architecture — is to keep authenticating and authorizing per request regardless of network path: VPN membership can still gate connectivity, but it should never be treated as a substitute for identity and posture checks on the request itself.
